questions.q: What is the name of the literary dialect used by Meerabai in her poetry, and which modern Hindi region does it historically belong to?
questions.a: The dialect is Braj Bhasha, historically spoken in the Braj region (Mathura-Vrindavan area) of present-day Uttar Pradesh. A wrong answer (e.g., "Awadhi" or "Khari Boli") reveals the student cannot distinguish between major medieval literary dialects, which is essential for recognizing why Meerabai's verb endings and vocabulary differ from modern standard Hindi.

questions.q: Explain why Meerabai chose to compose in Braj Bhasha rather than Sanskrit, and how this choice relates to the Bhakti movement's core philosophy.
questions.a: Meerabai used Braj Bhasha because the Bhakti movement emphasized direct, personal devotion accessible to common people, bypassing Sanskrit's priestly monopoly. A wrong answer focusing only on "she didn't know Sanskrit" or "it was her mother tongue" misses the socio-religious dimension: the deliberate democratization of spiritual expression through vernacular language, a hallmark of Nirguna and Saguna Bhakti traditions alike.

questions.q: In the line "vc r csfy iSQfy x;h] vk.kan&iQy gks;h", identify the verb forms "x;h" and "gks;h", state their modern Hindi equivalents, and name the grammatical tense/aspect they represent.
questions.a: "x;h" = "thī" (past habitual/feminine singular), "gks;h" = "huī" (past perfective/feminine singular). Both are feminine singular past forms in Braj Bhasha. A student who writes "thā/thī" for both or cannot distinguish habitual vs perfective aspect shows they are applying modern Hindi paradigms mechanically without recognizing Braj's distinct aspectual system.

questions.q: Compare the case marking in "esjs rks fxjèkj xksiky" (my Giridhar Gopal) and "nwèk dh eFkfu;k¡" (of the new love). Why does the first use no postposition while the second uses "dh"? What does this reveal about Braj Bhasha's case system?
questions.a: "esjs rks fxjèkj xksiky" uses the direct (nominative) case for the subject "Giridhar Gopal" with no postposition, while "nwèk dh eFkfu;k¡" uses the genitive postposition "dh" (of) showing possession. Braj Bhasha, like modern Hindi, marks only oblique cases with postpositions; the direct case remains unmarked. A wrong answer claiming "esjs" is a postposition or that both lines use the same case reveals confusion between pronoun case and noun case marking.

questions.q: Evaluate the effect of the repeated alliteration (anupras) in "valqou ty lhafp&lhafp] izse&csfy cks;h" on the poem's emotional intensity. Would the same effect be achieved in modern Khari Boli? Justify.
questions.a: The reduplicated "lhafp&lhafp" (wave after wave) and "izse&csfy" (love's longing) create sonic waves mimicking the overwhelming, repetitive nature of viraha (separation) longing. In Khari Boli, the phonetic inventory differs (e.g., loss of Braj's characteristic vowel length and consonant clusters), weakening the onomatopoeic resonance. A student who says "yes, alliteration works in any language" misses the phonological specificity: Braj's phonetics are integral to the aesthetic experience (rasa) of the poem.

questions.q: Compose a two-line couplet in Braj Bhasha style (using appropriate verb endings, vocabulary, and rhyme) expressing the idea: "My heart longs for the divine vision." Do not copy from the textbook.
questions.a: Example: "moro hiyo ḍole daraś kī ās, naina bane pīyasi pīyās." (My heart swings with hope of vision, eyes become thirsty with thirst.) A poor answer uses modern Hindi forms ("mera dil darta hai", "aankhein pyasi hain") showing inability to internalize Braj morphology (verb "ḍole" vs "ḍoltā hai", vocabulary "hiyo" vs "dil", rhyme "ās/pīyās").
